Tunica intima.description: The innermost layer, facing the blood. It is a single sheet of flat endothelial cells, which release nitric oxide to relax the vessel, on a thin layer of connective tissue. The internal elastic lamina, a sheet of elastin, separates it from the middle muscle layer.
clinical: Endothelial injury lets LDL cholesterol collect in the subendothelial layer, where it is oxidised and attracts inflammatory cells. This builds the fatty plaques of atherosclerosis.
A damaged endothelium makes less nitric oxide, so the artery constricts more readily and platelets stick to it more easily, promoting clots. This is an early step in cardiovascular disease.

Tunica media.description: The thick middle layer of smooth muscle cells, arranged in rings or a shallow spiral around the vessel, with elastic and collagen fibres between them; its cigar-shaped nuclei belong to these cells. Contraction narrows the artery to control blood flow and pressure, and the outer edge of the layer is the external elastic lamina, a thin elastic sheet.
clinical: Long-standing high blood pressure makes the smooth muscle of this layer thicken (hypertrophy) and the artery wall stiffen and remodel. This raises peripheral resistance and keeps blood pressure high.

This inflammatory disease damages the walls of medium-sized and small muscular arteries, with inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis of the arterial wall. It often causes small aneurysms and infarcts in the organs these arteries supply.

Tunica adventitia.description: The outer coat of connective tissue, mostly collagen with some elastic fibres and fibroblasts. It anchors the artery to the surrounding tissue and carries the small vessels (vasa vasorum) and nerves that supply the wall.

clinical: Sickle-shaped red cells are stiff and can block small vessels, causing pain and damage to the tissue they supply.
Neutrophils roll along inflamed endothelium, stick, and squeeze out into the tissue to fight infection; they are the first white cells to arrive in acute inflammation.

parts.description: The endothelium is the single layer of flat endothelial cells that lines the lumen of the artery and faces the blood. Its cells release nitric oxide, a gas that relaxes the smooth muscle of the wall, and prostacyclin, a signal made from fatty acids that discourages platelets from sticking together. In sections, look for thin, flattened nuclei that bulge slightly into the lumen, lying on the thin subendothelial layer.

The subendothelial layer is the thin sheet of loose connective tissue lying between the endothelium and the internal elastic lamina. It contains fine collagen fibrils, some elastic fibres and scattered cells, and in older arteries it often thickens with extra smooth muscle cells and matrix. In sections it appears as a pale, narrow zone between the flat endothelial nuclei and the wavy internal elastic lamina below.

The internal elastic lamina is a wavy, fenestrated sheet of elastin that forms the boundary between the intima and the media of a muscular artery. Its holes, called fenestrae, allow small molecules to diffuse through and let smooth muscle cells make direct contact with the endothelium. In sections it appears as a thin, wavy line, most clearly seen with an elastin stain such as Verhoeff-van Gieson, which colours elastic fibres black.

Smooth muscle nuclei are the elongated, cigar-shaped nuclei of the smooth muscle cells that make up the tunica media. Each cell has one central nucleus, and in a section these appear as dark purple, rod-shaped profiles scattered between the elastic and collagen fibres. Because the cells are arranged in rings or spirals, their nuclei run around the vessel, and they look wavy or corkscrew-shaped when the cell contracts.

The external elastic lamina is a thin sheet of elastin at the outer edge of the tunica media, where the smooth muscle layer meets the adventitia. It is usually less distinct and less continuous than the internal elastic lamina, so it is often hard to see in routine sections. An elastin stain such as Verhoeff-van Gieson shows it as a black, wavy line around the outside of the media.

The tunica adventitia is the outermost layer of the artery wall, a sheath of connective tissue that blends into the surrounding tissue. It is made mainly of type I collagen fibres, which run largely lengthwise along the vessel, with some elastic fibres and fibroblasts (the connective tissue cells). It anchors the artery to its surroundings and carries the vasa vasorum and nerves that supply the wall, plus lymphatic vessels that drain it. In sections it lies outside the external elastic lamina as a pinkish, fibrous layer.

Adventitial collagen bundles are the wavy bundles of type I collagen that make up most of the tunica adventitia, the outer coat of the artery. They run mainly along the length of the vessel, often in a shallow spiral, with elastic fibres between them. At normal blood pressure the bundles are slack and wavy, and they straighten and tighten only when the artery is stretched, which limits how far it can distend.

The vasa vasorum ('vessels of the vessels') are the tiny arteries, capillaries and venules that supply the wall of a larger artery. In a muscular artery they lie mainly in the adventitia, with some branches reaching the outer media, while the inner wall takes its oxygen and nutrients by diffusion from the blood in the lumen. In sections they appear as small, thin-walled vessel profiles scattered through the adventitia, some cut across and some running along it.

The venules of the vasa vasorum are the small, thin-walled vessels that collect blood from the capillaries of the outer artery wall. They lie beside the small arteries of the adventitia and drain into the larger veins nearby. Their walls are thinner than those of the neighbouring arteries and they lack a thick muscle coat, so in sections they can be told apart by their thin walls and relatively wide lumen.

Nervi vasorum are the nerve fibres of the vessel wall, mainly unmyelinated sympathetic (vasomotor) axons that run through the adventitia. Their varicosities, the swellings along the fibres, release noradrenaline into the surrounding tissue, which diffuses inwards and contracts the smooth muscle of the media by acting on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Because the fibres are so fine, they are seen clearly only with special stains such as silver impregnation or immunohistochemistry.

Perivascular fat is the layer of adipose tissue that surrounds the outside of an artery, lying just beyond the adventitia. Its fat cells (adipocytes) store energy, but the tissue is also active: it releases adipokines, chemical signals that in health help relax the vessel. In obesity it can become inflamed and encourage atherosclerosis. In sections it looks like clear fat tissue, with each cell appearing as a large, empty-looking space and a thin rim of cytoplasm pushing its nucleus to one side.

Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are the most numerous cells in the blood. They are biconcave discs with no nucleus, about 7.5 µm across, and this shape gives them a large surface for gas exchange and lets them squeeze through capillaries narrower than their own diameter. In sections they stand out as small, intensely pink discs without a nucleus, which makes them easy to tell apart from white cells.

A rolling leukocyte is a white blood cell, usually a neutrophil, that slows and tumbles along the endothelium (the lining of the vessel) during inflammation. Sticky surface proteins called selectins make it tether and roll, then adhesion proteins called integrins make it stop firmly. It then squeezes between endothelial cells into the tissue, a process called diapedesis, which happens mostly in postcapillary venules (small veins just after the capillaries). Its multilobed nucleus and pale, granular cytoplasm identify it in a section.
